title: Context-dependent consumptive and non-consumptive predator effects of omnivorous tadpoles based on body size and habitat shading
content:
Abstract

Despite previous treatment as herbivores, largely omnivorous tadpoles may exhibit both consumptive (CEs) and non-consumptive effects (NCEs), but the roles of additional biotic and abiotic factors in mediating these effects, such as body size and habitat shading, are poorly understood. We compared freshwater invertebrate abundance and community composition across tadpole body size and habitat shading treatments to assess whether these factors influence the strength of tadpole CEs and NCEs. Macroinvertebrate and zooplankton abundances and community composition were characterized in mesocosms with either large or small wood frog (Lithobates sylvaticus) tadpoles either shaded or not in separate CE (uncaged tadpole) and NCE (caged tadpole) treatments. Invertebrates were least abundant in mesocosms with larger tadpoles under shade. Macroinvertebrates suffered declines associated with CEs and NCEs, whereas zooplankton experienced positive NCEs but negative CEs. Our results suggest larger predators can predate more diverse prey (CEs) due to their wider gapes, but also that increased production of cues associated with predation risk can elicit stronger prey behavioral responses, such as changes in foraging time (NCEs). Predator body sizes and habitat shading are shifting with climate change, and such shifts may alter strength and direction of CEs and NCEs exerted by amphibians on freshwater invertebrates.
